Inside the model
How one token gets made
602dc565c645f77c: One question — how does an LLM produce an answer one token at a time, and where in that process is it slow and expensive?
e4805e8e33891986: Inference engineering is the work of running generative AI models faster, cheaper, and more reliably while keeping quality intact[1]. To do that, you need a feel for what happens inside the model. This page starts with a single matmul and climbs five steps: activation functions, tokens and sampling, attention and the KV cache, and Mixture of Experts (MoE). Each step has an experiment you can play with.

c984521fb20ea604: The analogy for this page — a restaurant kitchen
ce089f2dfcda6d05: Inference is a lot like a kitchen handling orders and sending out dishes: reading the order ticket (prefill), sending out one dish at a time (decode), the ingredient trays prepped in advance (KV cache), and assigning specialist cooks (MoE). For each step, we also note where the analogy breaks down. Source: *Inference Engineering* Sections 2.1–2.2<sup>[1]</sup>.
0f687b416b156b1e: Why you should know what's inside the model
7876a134594dcec2: Faster and cheaper, with quality unchanged
0bd8ba59ece101d6: The book defines inference engineering as making models fast, cheap, and trustworthy "without sacrificing quality." To know what you can cut, you have to know what does the work inside the model<sup>[1]</sup>.
30f7d058ccd561f1: Time gets spent in two places
aa986210040dcd54: Most inference time and resources go to building the KV cache in prefill and producing logits in decode. Both come down to running a large neural network<sup>[1]</sup>.
0b9151255d9a13df: With the same architecture, a well-optimized deployment can be used as is, even when size, variants, or fine-tuning differ. That's why you start by learning to read the architecture name line in config.json[1].
1e12b36fd6eb3716: Doctor's one line: to buy speed, first know where the time leaks.
61347064da0d21cf: The big picture — from order to next token
1097cf120ea292ed: Transformer-based generative models come in two branches. Autoregressive token generation predicts the next token from a sequence of tokens (LLMs), while iterative noise removal starts from random noise and refines the result through diffusion (image generation)[1]. This page covers the first, LLMs. Image generation continues in Section 2.3 of the book.
016c38da96feca7d: Append the chosen token to the end of the input and repeat until a stop token or max_tokens (decode)
f7603bb03b16bbf6: Prefill: process the whole input at once to build the KV cache
8d32c47f43cda30d: 0 Tokenize (chat template)1 Prefill → KV cache2 Decode: one forward pass = one token3 Logits → probabilities → draw4 Stop token · context window · max_tokens
bdd60c2adc165c98: An encoder turns input into an internal representation that carries meaning, and a decoder produces output from that representation. Today's LLMs are decoder-only; encoder-only models are rarer, like BERT-style embedding models. Whisper, the speech transcription model, is encoder-decoder[1].
87f9c8fc806dd7f6: 1950s hardware perceptrons → back-propagation leads to multilayer perceptrons → deep networks in the 2000s → 2012 AlexNet shows the power of GPUs → 2017 "Attention Is All You Need" introduces the transformer<sup>[1][2]</sup>.
2d5267c316d61277: Linear layers and matmul — the basic operation of neural networks
9a94914a1005d095: Model: y = xW + bEveryday: sauce blending ratio sheet
e2aabf7ab93c135e: Multiply the ingredient amounts (input) by the blend ratios (weights), add them up, and add a base seasoning (bias), and you get the sauce's taste score (output). Run it through two ratio sheets, and you get the same result from a single combined sheet made by multiplying the two in advance.
245f648d0df3352d: A node is a small program that multiplies its input by weights, adds a bias, and returns the result. Gather nodes and you get a layer. A linear layer multiplies an input vector by a weight matrix and adds a bias vector. Two linear layers in a row equal a single merged layer whose matrix is the product of theirs[1].
2ea97d57fdd1bfc3: Experiment ① — grid through two layers vs grid through one merged layer
da6c6414034a28c6: Seeing it in action — one point takes two paths
578d8a4855cf9074: Layer 1: y = xW₁ + b₁. Layer 2: z = yW₂ + b₂.
ecf2e39d3bce3bef: Put layer 1 into layer 2 and you get z = x(W₁W₂) + (b₁W₂ + b₂).
4198c058f8daa9b0: Set W₃ = W₁W₂ and b₃ = b₁W₂ + b₂, and z = xW₃ + b₃. Two layers have folded into one. That's why the two grids in the experiment above never differ by a hair.
ffc9cd5707e9f843: Most of an LLM's weights sit in linear layers like these, and the values in the matrices are set during training<sup>[1]</sup>.
61415e1c3cd04e72: Limit of this section: stack only linear layers, and no matter how deep, the model is equivalent to a single layer, so stacking means nothing. → The next section introduces a device that keeps the layers from folding.
61da915fc48d06cf: If x ∈ ℝ<sup>1×d</sup>, W₁ ∈ ℝ<sup>d×h</sup>, and W₂ ∈ ℝ<sup>h×k</sup>, then W₃ = W₁W₂ ∈ ℝ<sup>d×k</sup>. This follows from the associativity of matrix multiplication, (xW₁)W₂ = x(W₁W₂). Figure 2.3 in the book shows this calculation as is<sup>[1]</sup>.
d28ce0e037088bf6: I measured the gap between where the two paths land. With the numbers above and nothing in between, it's 0.
9e6c5869fc914399: Activation functions — bending layers so they don't fold
38c6daf60be3a1ef: Model: ReLU(x) = max(0, x)Fruit fly: firing threshold (supporting analogy)
d1eba450b70fcceb: A fruit fly neuron fires only when its input crosses a threshold. Input below the threshold simply disappears. It resembles ReLU in that it doesn't just "add the signal as is."
69ff5897f9ade021: Limitation: real neurons emit electrical pulses (spikes) and don't output values proportional to input the way ReLU does.
5f45414266df3b9d: Activation functions are nonlinear, so they stop matrix multiplications from folding into a single layer, and they are (almost) differentiable, which helps learning through back-propagation. ReLU returns x if x is greater than 0, and 0 otherwise. ReLU, SiLU, Swish, and SwiGLU are fast and easy to train<sup>[1]</sup>.
5381ce494f6e52c4: Experiment ② — separating a disc from a ring (8 hidden nodes)
20ea9f4671cff7f3: Seeing it in action — judge the validation dishes one at a time
49b2722ae006594c: Explanation — bent lines add up to a curve
ca08c9f12219fe33: Without an activation, even with a hidden layer, the whole model is equivalent to a single linear layer, so the boundary is one straight line. A disc and a ring can't be separated by a straight line.
55bed9af16129b2d: Scores are measured on validation points that were not used for training.
b7080053b733454e: Limit of this section: a neural network takes in only vectors of numbers and outputs only vectors of numbers. It can't take letters directly or answer in letters. → Next section: tokens.
f235c4ede179bf3b: Hidden h = φ(xW₁ + b₁), output p = σ(hW₂ + b₂). If φ is the identity function, then p = σ(x(W₁W₂) + …), so the boundary xW₃ + b₃ = 0 is a straight line. ReLU(z) = max(0, z), SiLU(z) = z·σ(z). Training: cross-entropy, full-batch gradient descent, learning rate 0.8, seeds 3 (weights), 5 (training), 77 (validation).
390b04a7c29743b1: Look at the hollow (validation) dot scores, not the training scores. Those are the real ones.
08c84ecbe1f05882: Tokens and picking the next token
e295cf6900e8749d: Model: logits → probabilities → drawEveryday: writing orders as menu numbers
aa228700f5c64448: The kitchen doesn't pass the customer's words along as they are. It writes them down as menu numbers and sends those to the line. Converting the numbers isn't done by a cook; a single table does it. Frequently ordered items get one number, and rare orders get several numbers strung together.
51bdb573090fb6cf: Limitation: humans choose the menu numbers, but a tokenizer's vocabulary is built from data and differs from model to model.
3e768b59693a89f4: A token is a number representing a piece of text. Today's LLMs use subword tokenization, so a token is either a whole word or part of a word. A tokenizer is a table that pairs strings with numbers without any neural network, and the model's output layer produces a logit vector as long as the vocabulary[1].
fe41555d30adfdae: The book's example — 6 words, 41 characters, 8 tokens
75c85b0e0d01f2b2: The token numbers are exactly as in Figure 2.5 of the book<sup>[1]</sup>. The uncommon word "Inference" is split into two tokens. The fewer tokens, the faster the same output gets finished.
a3873fd3d7ee8895: Experiment ③ — next token after "Inference engineering makes AI apps"
39a62b22c9ad62d4: Seeing it in action — write one token at a time (same temperature, top-k, top-p)
447476affb4c6232: Explanation — five steps to produce one token
d32be5158a55877d: The input (prompt, conversation, tool descriptions) is wrapped in a chat template, made into one line, and tokenized. This is step 0 of inference.
10aa9e580b1fd92a: The model produces a logit for every token in the vocabulary.
9a29149e718269e7: Normalizing the logits gives probabilities. Temperature adjusts the logits themselves before normalization.
4da5b9c53a3fe52d: top-k keeps only the top k by probability, while top-p keeps the smallest group whose probabilities add up to p, then normalizes again.
4298ed939e4d066f: Draw one at random according to the remaining probabilities. At temperature 0 or top-k 1, it always picks the highest-probability token. It ends when a stop token appears or the context window or max_tokens is reached<sup>[1]</sup>.
c56e36d18e711005: Limit of this section: to pick the next token, you have to look at all the earlier tokens. The longer the sentence, the more you need a mechanism for deciding what to look at and how much. → Next section: attention.
d630fe547ce4f76a: pᵢ = exp(zᵢ/T) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ/T). As T → 0, argmax. top-k: over the set S of the top k, pᵢ/Σ<sub>S</sub>p. top-p: the set where the cumulative sum in descending order first reaches at least p. For structured output (such as JSON), tools like logit bias are applied after the forward pass<sup>[1]</sup>.
2bf55fae02c8873e: Lowering "temperature" in a chatbot's settings makes answers always similar, and raising it makes them varied but off-base; this bar chart is why. Reasoning models produce an extra stream of thinking tokens before the answer, and the input, thinking, and output all have to fit within the context window together<sup>[1]</sup>.
5dd6cfd5fe411694: Limit of the analogy: real vocabularies exceed 100,000 tokens, and the 8-candidate bars show only the top slice as an example.
bd79d5ac3be9a55e: Fewer tokens means a smaller bill too. Tokenizer efficiency is a return on investment.
8c9b0a0b6f231b77: Attention and the KV cache — how earlier tokens get referenced
07cf9e7917b835ba: Model: softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)VEveryday: prepped ingredient trays
98716847ee9662fe: When an order comes in, all the ingredients are prepped first and stored in trays (prefill). Then each time a dish goes out, the prepped trays are taken out and used, and one more tray is stacked for the new dish (decode). Every dish isn't prepped from scratch.
48ff1cc1d348a5f9: Limitation: ingredients get used up, but the KV cache keeps growing per token and per layer, occupying GPU memory.
563bbe44a690e4aa: Attention weighs the current token (Q) against the representations of earlier tokens (K) to set weights, then blends the values of earlier tokens (V) by those amounts. The K and V of earlier tokens are stored in the KV cache in GPU memory so they don't have to be recomputed[1].
9053c0875435544f: Experiment ④-A — where "it" looks in the book's example (causal mask)
e604e555948945e8: Experiment ④-B — K·V computation count with and without the KV cache
ccf679cdaba98858: Seeing it in action — prefill and decode in the kitchen
f032e1f43ff1af00: Explanation — Q, K, V and two stages
51f222b946431017: Q (query): the representation of the token being made or revised now. K (key): the representations of earlier tokens. V (value): the computed values of earlier tokens[1].
ea4ec1878f03656a: LLMs apply a causal mask to self-attention (where Q, K, and V come from the same sequence) so that later tokens can't be seen. Image and multimodal models also use cross-attention[1].
5dde51b2ea4d15af: Attention layers run multiple heads in parallel. Each head can take on a different relationship, such as subject-verb agreement or reference<sup>[1]</sup>.
8cc8a1b1e8431c18: Attention looks at the relationship between the current token and all earlier tokens, so it takes quadratic time in sentence length. The book explains that thanks to the KV cache it effectively runs linearly, because when making a token, the K and V of earlier tokens are pulled from the cache rather than recomputed<sup>[1]</sup>.
06dfa9a4b3c08aaa: The KV cache is built during prefill, used and updated during decode, and by default lives in GPU memory. Storing and reusing it is a major topic in Section 5.3 of the book<sup>[1]</sup>.
19288686cb594ab9: Limit of this section: the largest share of weights is not in attention but in the feed-forward (linear) layers. Every token has to pass through this huge matrix in full. → Next section: Mixture of Experts, which uses only some of them.
36701349553347c0: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V (Vaswani et al. 2017; the book follows the notation of Dao et al. 2022)<sup>[1][2][3]</sup>. The arithmetic for experiment ④-B: with prompt length P and N output tokens, without cache = Σ<sub>t=1..N</sub>(P+t) = NP + N(N+1)/2, with cache = P + N. The dot-product work at each step (P+t times) is the same in both cases; what the cache reduces is the recomputation of the K·V of earlier tokens.
44b51ee40b10ea0e: When you paste in a long document, the wait before the first character appears is prefill, and the characters that then stream out are decode.
ae4f8e10a93e2dde: Limit of the analogy: real service latency also mixes in other factors, such as queueing and the network.
1f7148079543ec36: The KV cache consumes GPU memory in proportion to the number of concurrent requests × the context length. When designing a service, budget for "cache memory" separately from "weight memory."
e65b37d5a31e9d43: Limit of the analogy: actual size depends on the number of layers, KV heads, and precision; this page counts only the cells.
5a7e0dfbaf536bfe: Doctor's one line: once prepped, ingredients don't get prepped again. That's the KV cache.
d27093dba23b91b8: Mixture of Experts (MoE) — small experts instead of one giant matrix
4579ee90ccdac115: Model: router picks 8 of 128 expertsEveryday: head chef assigns specialist cooks
316670eb00cd06de: 3Main version of the architecture within the family
3e0c69b1673b8d89: CausalLMCausal language model: sees only earlier tokens and predicts the next
bab8fd93fb762a06: This is the book's explanation as is<sup>[1]</sup>. A causal language model differs from a masked language model, which fills in blanks using context from both sides, and today's generative LLMs are all causal language models. Within the same architecture there are multiple sizes (e.g., Llama 8B and 70B), base and instruct variants, and fine-tuning such as LoRA, but the architecture itself doesn't change.
424478f8192060ea: Instead of one cook making every dish, there are 128 specialist cooks, and the head chef (router) calls on only 8 for each dish. With one customer, only 8 cooks are busy. But when dinner service brings a crowd, each dish calls different cooks, so in the end almost everyone is busy.
93ccda600187d009: Limitation: the real router chooses again at each of the 94 layers, not once per dish. And idle experts still have to be loaded in memory.
1ce2c8d87f85a500: MoE adds sparsity to linear layers. Instead of one large matrix, it has hundreds of small matrices (experts) and activates only a few per input. Qwen3-235B-A22B uses 22 billion of its 235 billion parameters per request, selecting 8 of 128 experts at each of 94 layers. In batch inference, different experts switch on for each request, so you should assume nearly all parameters are active<sup>[1]</sup>.
091af600f6c34899: Experiment ⑤ — one layer, 128 experts, changing the batch size
b88b223245d3bd59: Seeing it in action — the head chef sends tokens to experts
0d8d4aaaea36cade: Explanation — used alone vs. on a server
f37ce8e041b32bf1: The density of a neural network is determined by the number of connections between layers. The denser it is, the more information it holds; the sparser it is, the less computation and memory it uses<sup>[1]</sup>.
8bb26b5b89026480: Running a single request alone, MoE is very efficient because few parameters are active (local, single request).
60fd86467f427588: As the batch grows, the experts selected differ from token to token, so the union of switched-on experts grows quickly. In the experiment above, a batch of 64 switches on most of them.
4569b26e172c8a82: That's why large-scale services keep the sparsity useful with expert parallelism, splitting experts across multiple GPUs. In the book's example in Figure 2.9, 8 GPUs each handle 16 experts, and the router is replicated on each GPU[1].
7f6e8e8b85d70332: Models under 32B, especially under 8B, tend to be efficient with a traditional dense structure. For narrow-domain models like tab autocomplete, the whole model is effectively one expert, so MoE gains little<sup>[1]</sup>.
8437b8ea91c52a9b: Limit of this section: you can't count server cost by active parameter count alone. You have to consider batch, parallelization method, and memory together. That calculation (the compute-to-byte ratio and bottlenecks) continues in Section 2.4 and Section 5.4.2 of the book.
f48806b81e65800e: Don't look at the "22B active" label and prepare only 22B worth of GPU memory. All the experts have to fit in memory, and as the batch grows, nearly all expert weights get read at every step.
61ad211d302e9dbf: Limit of the analogy: the actual routing distribution varies by model and data, and the degree of skew on this page is an assumption.
fe4d61819b2b7d61: Conditions: a Qwen3-style MoE layer (128 experts, 8 per token), with 64 tokens arriving together in one decode step on the service server (batch 64). At each of the 94 layers, we measure "the fraction of experts switched on in this step" and compare it with each character's prediction. The judging criterion is prediction error (smaller is better).
11309290910f0529: "With 64 guests, nearly every cook gets called in. Assume they all work and plan memory accordingly."
ed5509f345814499: This calculation is an illustrative model. The routing scores were made from random values with seed 2026 plus differences in each expert's popularity. Set the batch to 1, and Money-Robo's 6.25% comes out exactly right. You can check this yourself in Experiment ⑤ above.
0e8bd449d2e723f5: Summary — the five steps at a glance
c4ef5afa42f7b338: Limit (why it called the next step)
8e2226f151973956: Stacking still folds into one layer
ebfe6f5abdee98d7: Handles numbers only, doesn't know letters
4c1108444b865255: Text ↔ numbers, picks the next token as probabilities
4475086f81dc729f: Relationships with earlier tokens, continues writing without recomputation
71f50be70f54291a: Passes through the linear layers, which hold most weights, in full every time
96597896fcc31826: Uses only some experts per token
021c0c6fdb7d8931: In batches almost all are on; memory is needed for all
59974e23ba95cb50: The output a hidden layer produces that the next layer reads. In text, dimensions are increased to hundreds or thousands; in images, millions of pixels are reduced<sup>[1]</sup>.
e283ce32370fbc7e: The input layer that turns tokens into embeddings, and the output layer that turns the hidden state into logits the size of the vocabulary<sup>[1]</sup>.
45761c053bf8f241: The feed-forward (MLP) holds most of the trainable weights, and attention comes second. Normalization and activations are at the level of rounding error in size<sup>[1]</sup>.
b39cfcac0bcfb084: A file of a few dozen lines found in every LLM on Hugging Face. It lists the architecture name and the sizes of layers and vectors<sup>[1]</sup>.
6dc1ba504891cbf2: The blend-ratio sheet analogy resembles only the "multiply and add" of matrices. Real matrices are thousands by thousands in size, and their values are set by training.
dd41375a69ff7511: The fruit fly firing threshold resembles only in that it "bends." Neural networks didn't imitate a fruit fly's brain; they only borrowed the skeleton.
daea16fb92dd0628: Attention borrows only the name from human focused attention. In practice it is dot products and softmax computation.
6e237a08995c340b: The "cook labor cost" in the kitchen analogy resembles MoE's computation, but it differs in that idle experts still occupy GPU memory.
82237dc6c6330af6:
Three lines to sum up today.
① An activation function is what makes stacking layers meaningful. ② Inference builds the KV cache with prefill and emits one token at a time with decode. ③ MoE's sparsity is large when used alone, and on a batch server it only works with expert parallelism.
